newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Payrolls blight U.S. outlook.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Payrolls blight U.S. outlook.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries will tackle most of this week's weighty data with ease, outperforming European markets on signs of slowing economic growth, analysts said on Monday.
But they said the bullish tone could do an about-face on Friday, as the crucial but volatile payrolls data prove to be the Achilles' heel of Treasuries yet again.

The raft of data, which includes the employment cost index on Tuesday, third quarter GDP on Wednesday and October payrolls on Friday, will determine whether the Federal Reserve needs to act on interest rates in the fourth quarter, economists said.

"If we get a reasonably good employment cost index and GDP data and home sales, there is scope for the market to move higher. Spreads will narrow against other markets," said Adam Chester at Yamaichi International in London.

According to a Reuters poll, economists expect the U.S. employment cost index, a measure of wage inflation and important indicator of future inflationary pressures, to rise 0.8 percent in the third quarter, unchanged from the second quarter rate.
Third quarter GDP on Wednesday is seen rising 1.9 percent, a significant slowdown from the 4.7 percent growth in the second quarter and showing more evidence U.S. growth is cooling.

Chester, an international bond strategist, said the data could prompt the 10-year Treasury/Bund spread to narrow to 55 basis points by Friday, ahead of the payrolls data, from its current 64 basis points.
"We recommend moving to a neutral or short position (in Treasuries) going into Friday's payrolls number because all the good news ends there," he said.
Non-farm payrolls data are a key element in determining labour market tightness and are closely watched by markets for signs of future inflationary pressures.
Economists expect payrolls to rise by 239,000 in October after September's surprise 40,000 drop. Unemployment is expected to come in steady at 5.2 percent.
Daiwa economist Katy Peters agreed the payrolls number on Friday may spook investors into a sell-off.
"Our feeling is that most of the week the Treasury market will remain range-bound in the 110-112 range," said Peters.
December T-bonds at 1320 GMT were at 111-02, up 2/32.

"But we think non-farm payrolls will be larger than the market expects, at around 250,000...and on balance the report will be negative for Treasuries. It will call for some reassessment of the outlook for interest rates."
This reassessment will prompt Treasuries to underperform Bunds in the weeks ahead, Peters added. "Ten-year spreads could push up to around 70 within a week and a half," she said.
ABN AMRO Hoare Govett economist Brian Venables agreed Treasuries had upside potential this week.
"The U.S. definitely has more potential to go up, spreads could narrow," he said. "We're looking to a 10-year Bund spread in the mid 50s if the data go well."
He said payrolls were the wild card and could upset the market. "But we have to assume that the economy has been slowing down and payrolls can only confirm that."

Other data this week include consumer confidence on Tuesday, home sales and the Fed's Beige Book on Wednesday, personal income and week jobless claims on Thursday and the National Association of Purchasing Management index on Friday.
After all that, obstacles in the weeks ahead will keep a lid on any gains in Treasuries, economists said.
U.S. elections on November 5 and a Federal Open Market Committee meeting on November 13 will keep investors sidelined, economists said.
Both Venables and Yamaichi's Chester were unenthusiastic about the performance of Treasuries in the longer term.

"We're coming into a crucial period for the U.S. economy with the key Christmas retail sales period ahead," said Chester, adding this could push economic growth up to around 3.0 percent in the fourth quarter. "In the long term we're more negative on inflation," he said.

Venables agreed growth was unlikely to be as weak as expected between now and the end of the year. This, coupled with steady Bunds, meant the spread had the potential widen out to around 90 basis points by the first quarter of 1997, he said.
